lead: A projection drops a vector perpendicularly onto a subspace and keeps the closest point. That single idea solves two problems. It tells you the part of b that lies inside a plane or a line. It also rescues an inconsistent system Ax = b: when no x fits exactly, least squares chooses x so that Ax is the closest reachable point to b. The same calculation fits a line to data, removes noise from sensor readings, and appears inside GPS and machine-learning code.
prereq: You need: inner products and norms (5.1), orthogonal complements (5.3), Gram–Schmidt (5.4), column space (Unit 2), and solving square systems (Unit 1).

sections.h3: Projection onto a line or a subspace

blocks.text: Take a vector b and a subspace W. The point of W closest to b is the orthogonal projection of b on W, written p. If W is the line through one nonzero vector a, then p is the part of b along a:

blocks.where: b and a are vectors, a ≠ 0; ⟨b,a⟩ is their inner product, a single number; ‖a‖ is the length of a, so ‖a‖² = ⟨a,a⟩.

blocks.text: The leftover e = b − p is perpendicular to a. The vectors p and e form a right triangle with b, so ‖b‖² = ‖p‖² + ‖e‖².
For a subspace with orthonormal basis e₁, …, e<sub>k</sub>, add the parts along each basis vector:

blocks.where: e<sub>i</sub> are orthonormal basis vectors of W; Q is the n×k matrix with the e<sub>i</sub> as columns; Qᵀb gives the k coefficients.

blocks.text: Best approximation: for every w in W with w ≠ p, ‖b−p‖ < ‖b−w‖. Write b−w = (b−p)+(p−w). The vector p−w lies in W, and b−p is orthogonal to W, so Pythagoras gives ‖b−w‖² = ‖b−p‖² + ‖p−w‖² > ‖b−p‖².
The projection matrix P = QQᵀ has three properties: P² = P, Pᵀ = P, and P projects every vector onto col(Q). The first follows from QᵀQ = I, since P² = QQᵀQQᵀ = Q(QᵀQ)Qᵀ = QQᵀ = P.

sections.h3: Least squares and the normal equations

blocks.text: When Ax = b has no solution, choose x to make ‖Ax − b‖ as small as possible. This is the least squares problem. As x runs over all k-vectors, Ax fills the column space of A. The best possible Ax is therefore the projection p of b onto col(A).
At the minimum the residual e = b − Ax is orthogonal to col(A). Every column of A lies in col(A), so Aᵀe = 0. Hence Aᵀ(b−Ax) = 0, which gives the normal equations:

blocks.where: A is m×k; x is the k×1 vector of unknowns; b is m×1. AᵀA is k×k and Aᵀb is k×1.

blocks.text: If the columns of A are independent, AᵀA is invertible and the solution x̂ = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb is unique. If columns are dependent, AᵀA has no inverse and many x can give the same best p.

items: Solve the k×k system AᵀAx = Aᵀb.
Compute the residual e = b − p.
Check Aᵀe = 0. If A has orthonormal columns, AᵀA = I and x̂ = Aᵀb.

blocks.text: The vector x̂ holds the coefficients of the fit, not the data values. In a line fit x̂ = (c₀, c₁)ᵀ. The vector p = Ax̂ holds the predicted y-values at the given x-values. The residual e = b − p holds the errors: observed minus predicted.

Least squares minimizes the sum of squared errors ‖e‖² = e₁² + … + e<sub>m</sub>². A zero residual means the data lie exactly on the model. A nonzero residual is normal and does not mean the arithmetic is wrong.

Check your answer with two tests. First, Aᵀe = 0: the residual is perpendicular to every column. Second, p lies in col(A) because p = Ax̂. These tests catch most sign and algebra slips. The residual sum of squares is the smallest possible value of ‖Ax−b‖². It measures how much of b is outside col(A). If the model is rich enough to contain b, e = 0 and the system is consistent.

figure.caption: The target b is projected to p in the column space; the leftover e is perpendicular to every column, which gives the normal equations.

spec.title: Projection and least squares
spec.aria: A left-to-right flow from the target vector b to its projection p in the column space, then to the residual, then to the normal equations.

examples.question: Fit the line y = c₀ + c₁x to the three points (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 4) by least squares. Find c₀ and c₁, write the fitted line, compute the residual vector e = b − Ac, and verify Aᵀe = 0.
steps: Put the unknowns in c = (c₀, c₁)ᵀ. Each data point gives one row [1, x], so A = [[1,0],[1,1],[1,2]] and b = (1, 2, 4)ᵀ.
Compute AᵀA. Top-left = 1+1+1 = 3. Top-right = 0+1+2 = 3. Bottom-right = 0²+1²+2² = 5. So AᵀA = [[3,3],[3,5]].
Compute Aᵀb. First entry = 1+2+4 = 7. Second entry = 0·1+1·2+2·4 = 10. So Aᵀb = (7, 10)ᵀ.
Solve the normal equations 3c₀ + 3c₁ = 7 and 3c₀ + 5c₁ = 10. Subtract: 2c₁ = 3, so c₁ = 3/2 = 1.5.
examples.answer: The least squares line is y = 5/6 + (3/2)x ≈ 0.8333 + 1.5x, with residual e = (1/6, −1/3, 1/6)ᵀ and Aᵀe = (0, 0)ᵀ.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction
A = [[Fraction(1), Fraction(0)], [Fraction(1), Fraction(1)], [Fraction(1), Fraction(2)]]
b = [Fraction(1), Fraction(2), Fraction(4)]
ata00 = sum(row[0]*row[0] for row in A)
ata01 = sum(row[0]*row[1] for row in A)
ata11 = sum(row[1]*row[1] for row in A)
atb0 = sum(A[i][0]*b[i] for i in range(3))
atb1 = sum(A[i][1]*b[i] for i in range(3))
det = ata00*ata11 - ata01*ata01
c0 = (atb0*ata11 - ata01*atb1)/det
c1 = (ata00*atb1 - ata01*atb0)/det
print(float(c0))
print(float(c1))
e = [b[i] - (A[i][0]*c0 + A[i][1]*c1) for i in range(3)]
for val in e:
    print(float(val))
print(float(sum(e)))
print(float(sum(A[i][1]*e[i] for i in range(3))))

traps: Writing AAᵀx = b or Ax = Aᵀb. The correct left multiplier is Aᵀ: AᵀAx = Aᵀb.
Assuming AᵀA is always invertible. It is invertible only when the columns of A are independent; otherwise least squares has many solutions.
Using ⟨b,a⟩/‖a‖ instead of ⟨b,a⟩/⟨a,a⟩. The denominator is the squared length, not the length.
Setting the residual e to zero. e is zero only when Ax = b is consistent; in least squares e is orthogonal to the columns, not zero in general.
Confusing the coefficient vector x with the projection p = Ax. x has one entry per unknown; p has one entry per data point.

quiz.q: State the three matrix properties of an orthogonal projection matrix P.
quiz.a: P² = P (idempotent), Pᵀ = P (symmetric), and P maps every vector onto col(Q), the subspace it projects on. When Q has orthonormal columns, P is written explicitly as P = QQᵀ.

quiz.q: Write the normal equations for least squares with matrix A and vector b.
Why is the least squares residual b − Ax orthogonal to every column of A?
quiz.a: At the minimum, moving x along any column direction cannot reduce the length. The derivative condition is Aᵀ(b−Ax) = 0, so the residual is orthogonal to all columns.

quiz.q: What happens to the least squares solution if the columns of A are dependent?
quiz.a: AᵀA is not invertible. There are infinitely many minimizers or no unique x, though the projection p = Ax is unique.

quiz.q: Project b = (2, 3) onto a = (1, 1). Give p and e.
For data (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 5), set up AᵀA and Aᵀb for the line y = c₀ + c₁x, then solve.
quiz.a: AᵀA = [[3,3],[3,5]], Aᵀb = (10,13)ᵀ. The equations give c₁ = 1.5 and c₀ = 11/6 ≈ 1.8333.

quiz.q: If Q has orthonormal columns, show that the normal equations reduce to x = Qᵀb.
quiz.a: QᵀQ = I, so QᵀQx = Qᵀb becomes x = Qᵀb.

quiz.q: Explain why P = QQᵀ is symmetric and idempotent.
quiz.a: Pᵀ = (QQᵀ)ᵀ = QQᵀ = P. Also P² = QQᵀQQᵀ = Q(QᵀQ)Qᵀ = QQᵀ = P.

beyond: Not for the exam. Least squares is the computational core of linear regression, signal denoising and computer vision. Large systems are not solved with (AᵀA)⁻¹; libraries use QR or SVD because they are more stable (5.6, 5.7). Ridge regression adds λ‖x‖² to control unstable fits. Search terms: normal equations, QR least squares, ridge regression, pseudo-inverse.
